city.name: Boston
summary: In 1775 Boston was a town of about 15,000 on the Shawmut peninsula, joined to the mainland by a thin neck of land. Merchants' wharves ran out into the harbour, and the town was crowded with brick and clapboard houses, churches and taverns.

It was the centre of resistance to British rule: the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party, then a British army under siege for eleven months until Washington's guns on Dorchester Heights forced it out in March 1776.
city.note: Shoreline after the Leventhal Map & Education Center's 1795 Boston shoreline; streets, wharves and the Mill Pond from OpenHistoricalMap (both CC0). Houses between the streets are generated; landmarks after surviving buildings and period plans.

properties.name: Boston Common
description: The town's cow pasture since 1634. From 1768 British regiments camped here, and in April 1775 the troops for Lexington and Concord formed up on it.

properties.name: Old State House (Town House)
description: The seat of royal government, built in 1713. The Boston Massacre happened in the street outside its east front in March 1770, and the Declaration of Independence was read from its balcony in July 1776.

properties.name: Faneuil Hall
description: Market below, meeting hall above, given to the town by the merchant Peter Faneuil in 1742. Samuel Adams and others spoke here against British taxes, earning it the name 'the Cradle of Liberty'.

properties.name: Old North Church (Christ Church)
description: Boston's tallest steeple. On the night of 18 April 1775 two lanterns were hung here, the signal that British troops were crossing by water to Charlestown.

properties.name: Old South Meeting House
description: The largest building in colonial Boston. On 16 December 1773 some 5,000 people met here before the Tea Party; the British later used it as a riding school.

properties.name: King's Chapel
description: The first Anglican church in Puritan Boston, rebuilt in granite in 1754. Its tower was never given the spire that was planned.

properties.name: Province House
description: The royal governor's mansion, where General Gage planned the march on Concord.

properties.name: Paul Revere House
description: Home of the silversmith Paul Revere, who rode to Lexington on the night of 18 April 1775. Built about 1680, it is the oldest house in downtown Boston.

properties.name: Hancock Manor
description: John Hancock's granite mansion on Beacon Street, looking over the Common. Hancock was the richest man in Boston and signed the Declaration first.

properties.name: Granary Burying Ground
description: Where Samuel Adams, John Hancock, Paul Revere and the victims of the Boston Massacre are buried.

properties.name: Long Wharf
description: A third of a mile of wharf running straight out from King Street into the harbour, lined with warehouses. British troops landed here in 1768.

properties.name: Griffin's Wharf
description: Where the Tea Party happened on 16 December 1773: colonists dressed as Mohawks threw 342 chests of East India Company tea into the harbour.

properties.name: Liberty Tree
description: The elm where the Sons of Liberty gathered from 1765. British soldiers cut it down in August 1775.

properties.name: British lines on Boston Neck
description: Earthworks across the narrow neck, the only road out of Boston, held by the British through the siege.

properties.name: Redoubt on Breed's Hill
description: Dug by about 1,200 Massachusetts men in a single night. On 17 June 1775 it fell to the third British assault, at the cost of over a thousand British casualties: the Battle of Bunker Hill.

properties.name: Dorchester Heights forts
description: Built overnight on 4 to 5 March 1776 with cannon dragged from Fort Ticonderoga. With guns commanding the harbour, the British evacuated Boston on 17 March.

properties.name: Charlestown
description: A town of about 2,700 across the river. British shells set it alight during the Battle of Bunker Hill and almost all of it burned.
